new_statements.quote: 80. The phenomena of accent are, by the Hindu grammarians of all ages alike, described and treated as depending on a variation of tone or pitch; of any difference of stress involved, they make no account. [...] 95. On the place of the accented syllable in a Sanskrit word there is no restriction whatever depending upon either the number or the quantity of the preceding or following syllables. The accent rests where the rules of inflection or derivation or composition place it, without regard to any thing else.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Old Indic (Vedic) has a musical pitch accent (udātta = high tone), one per word, whose position is lexically and morphologically determined (by inflection, derivation, composition) and may fall on any syllable regardless of syllable count or weight; there is no phonologically fixed or weight-sensitive word stress. Corroborated by Macdonell 1916:448, 451 ('a musical one, depending mainly on pitch'; 'one main accent only'), Wackernagel 1896 §244-245, and Ryan 2026:1 ('It can (and frequently does) occur on any syllable of the word, regardless of length.. lexically distinctive and largely unpredictable in roots'). Later (post-Vedic/modern) Sanskrit pronunciation replaced this with a Latin-type quantity-sensitive stress: penult if heavy, otherwise antepenult, otherwise the fourth-from-last (Wackernagel 1896 §254 p. 296; Macdonell 1910:77 n.2; Whitney §96) — that is not the Old Indic accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None reported; the svarita is a predictable falling 'enclitic' tone on the syllable after the udātta (Whitney §81, 85; Macdonell 1916:448), not a secondary accent. Some words carry two accents: dative infinitives in -tavai and some dual/genitive compounds (Whitney §94; Macdonell 1916:452 §7).
new_statements.exceptions: Enclitic particles and pronoun forms are always unaccented; vocatives and finite verbs in main clauses lose their accent unless sentence-/pāda-initial (Whitney §92-93; Macdonell 1916:452-453 §8; Ryan 2026:1). Some words have more than one accented syllable (Whitney §94). Independent svarita arises from an accented i/u becoming y/v (Whitney §83).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent as marked in the Vedic saṃhitās and taught by the native grammarians; Whitney §92 states it 'is essentially a system of word-accent only', with the pāda treated as a sentence for accentuation. Macdonell 1916 notes the hemistich is the unit for marking, while the Padapāṭha gives each word its own natural accent. Ryan 2026 treats the accent as purely tonal (restricted tone system), not stress.
new_statements.identity_note: oldi1244 is a Glottolog Bookkeeping node ('Old Indic', pseudo-ISO qmx, no family/coordinates, 0 descriptive refs) whose Glottolog link points to Wikipedia 'Old Indo-Aryan' (Wikidata Q118976896). Old Indo-Aryan = Vedic Sanskrit (Glottolog dialect vedi1234) plus Classical Sanskrit (Glottolog language sans1269, ISO san). All sources here describe Vedic Sanskrit; the same material is already If sans1269 is (or becomes) a catalog entry, oldi1244 should be merged into it or marked as a duplicate bookkeeping key rather than counted as a distinct language. The later Latin-type stress (Wackernagel §254) applies to post-Vedic / modern recitation pronunciation, not to Old Indic proper.

sources.locator: §80, p. 28 and §95, p. 33 (chapter II, section IV 'Accent')
sources.note: §80 p.28: accent is described by all Indian grammarians as pitch, 'of any difference of stress involved, they make no account'; §95 p.33: no restriction whatever on the place of the accented syllable depending on number or quantity of syllables, it rests where inflection/derivation/composition place it; §96 p.33: place undetermined for much vocabulary, Europeans pronounce by the Latin rule.

sources.citation: Ryan, Kevin. 2026. The role of pitch accent in Vedic Sanskrit poetics. Phonological Data and Analysis 8, e5, 1-26. DOI 10.1017/S2642182825000066 (CC-BY 4.0).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: p.1: Vedic is 'commonly known as a pitch accent language', accent 'arguably purely tonal'; each word has exactly one accent (exceptions: vocatives, main-clause finite verbs, clitics; double accent in -tavái infinitives and some compounds); 'Accent is not restricted to a window.. It can (and frequently does) occur on any syllable of the word, regardless of length'; 'Vedic accent is lexically distinctive and largely unpredictable in roots'; p.6: system privative and culminative.

sources.citation: Perry, J. Joseph & Bert Vaux. 2018. Vedic Sanskrit accentuation and readjustment rules. In Petrosino, Cerrone & van der Hulst (eds.), From Sounds to Structures, 266-294. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. Accepted MS, Cambridge Apollo DOI 10.17863/CAM.70756.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: pp.270-271: texts mark svarita (fall) and sannatara (low) around the high-pitched udātta syllable; surface accent derives from underlying lexical accents of stems and endings (leftmost wins), i.e. morphologically/lexically determined pitch accent.

sources.citation: Kiparsky, Paul. 2010. Compositional vs. paradigmatic approaches to accent and ablaut. Proc. 21st UCLA Indo-European Conference (author preprint).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Word accent computed 'from the lexically specified accentual features of their constituent morphemes'; Basic Accentuation Principle: leftmost lexical accent wins, otherwise left edge of an unaccented domain. Theoretical, not a descriptive statement.

sources.citation: Macdonell, Arthur A. 1916. A Vedic Grammar for Students. Oxford: Clarendon Press. Appendix III 'The Vedic Accent', §§1, 6-8, pp. 448-453.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: p.448: 'The Vedic, like the ancient Greek, accent was a musical one, depending mainly on pitch', three pitch levels udatta/svarita/anudatta; p.451 §6: 'Every Vedic word is, as a rule, accented and has one main accent only', the udatta 'generally rests on the same syllable as it did in the Indo-European period'; §7 double accent in -tavai infinitives and dvandvas; §8 enclitics, vocatives and main-clause verbs unaccented.

sources.citation: Macdonell, Arthur A. 1910. Vedic Grammar (Grundriss der indo-arischen Philologie und Altertumskunde I.4). Strassburg: Trübner. III. Accent, §83 'General character of Vedic accent', pp. 76-78.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: p.77: 'The Vedic accent, like that of ancient Greece, was of an essentially musical nature', no influence on metre, though 'accompanied by some stress'; three pitch degrees; p.77 n.2: after the beginning of our era it changed to a stress accent 'regulated by the quantity of the last two or three syllables, much as in Latin'.

sources.citation: Wackernagel, Jacob. 1896. Altindische Grammatik, I: Lautlehre. Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht. §§243-245 pp. 281-285; §254 pp. 296-297.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: §244 p.284: 'Der Akzent.. ist ein wesentlich musikalischer. Die Theoretiker sprechen immer nur von dessen Höhe, nie von dessen Stärke'; §245 p.285: 'Ein altindisches Wort hat entweder den Udātta oder den Svarita als Hauptton, oder es hat gar keinen Hauptton'; §254 p.296: in today's pronunciation an expiratory accent 'gleich geregelt wie der lateinische', except that with short penult and antepenult the fourth-from-last is stressed; p.297 refers to the older accent as 'auf beliebige Silben fallender'.
